analysis.one_liner: Bans most noncompete agreements between employers and workers nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Scott Peters with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, was referred to two House committees in January 2020 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for employers to enter into, enforce, or threaten noncompete agreements — contracts that stop employees from taking a similar job or working for a competitor after they leave. It would let the Federal Trade Commission treat violations as unfair business practices and let the Labor Department investigate complaints and fine violators up to $5,000 a week, paid to the affected worker. It also gives workers their own right to sue in federal court for damages and attorney's fees. Narrow exceptions would still allow noncompetes tied to the sale of a business, a partnership breakup, and senior executives with large severance packages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers covered by noncompete agreements, which the bill's own findings say may include roughly 1 in 5 American workers. Ending the agreements means they can take a new job in their field, negotiate higher pay against competing offers, and start businesses without fear of being sued. The bill's findings argue noncompetes reduce wages, restrict mobility, and slow innovation.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids noncompete agreements entered after enactment and makes entering into, enforcing, or threatening one illegal, except in limited cases [S2, S3].
Employers must post a workplace notice of the ban, so workers learn their rights [S2, S3].

Enforcement runs through the FTC as an unfair business practice, and through the Department of Labor, which must investigate complaints and can win civil fines up to $5,000 per week of violation paid to the aggrieved worker; workers can also sue on their own for damages and attorney's fees [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use noncompete agreements to keep workers from leaving or to hold down wages. They lose a cheap tool for retaining staff and would have to compete for workers with pay, benefits, or better conditions. Companies buying or selling businesses and top executives negotiating sale-related severance keep limited noncompete rights.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies only to agreements entered after enactment, so noncompetes already signed remain in force [S3].

The exceptions for business sales, partnership dissolutions, and senior executives with severance deals leave room for employers to restructure agreements around the ban, and nondisclosure and trade-secret agreements remain fully allowed, which can function much like a noncompete in practice [S3].
Enforcement depends on FTC and Labor Department action and on individual workers finding lawyers; the bill sets no new funding for either agency's enforcement role [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is large and broad: an estimated one-fifth of the workforce, spanning many industries and income levels, gains freedom to change jobs and leverage for raises. The exceptions are narrow enough that the ban is meaningful, though the carve-outs for business sales and executives and the survival of NDAs mean employers keep tools that can achieve similar ends. The bigger design weakness is that existing agreements are untouched. On balance the bill would shift power from employers toward workers at modest cost to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Energy and Commerce and Education and Labor committees after referral in January 2020; neither committee scheduled a hearing or markup, and it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on January 29, 2020, joined by Reps. Mike Gallagher, a Republican, and Anna Eshoo, a Democrat [S1, S3].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Education and Labor Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that use noncompete agreements to hold down wages and block job changes are better off; workers bound by noncompetes gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, so sponsorship crossed party lines, but no chamber vote ever tested broader support.

industries.note: Noncompetes are a standard tool across healthcare, tech, staffing, and many other sectors for keeping workers from leaving and for holding down pay. The bill would void new agreements and fine violators, forcing these employers to retain workers through pay and conditions instead [S2, S3].

industries.industry: Business sellers and buyers (franchise and business-sale market)
industries.note: The bill preserves noncompetes tied to the sale of a business, a partnership breakup, or senior executives with qualifying severance, so deal-making noncompetes remain a normal part of buying and selling companies [S3].

industries.industry: Employment law firms and compliance services
industries.note: The ban and its notice, reporting, and enforcement provisions would generate compliance work for employers and enforcement or defense work for lawyers, though workers' new private right of action also opens a source of cases [S3].
